title: Selling a story that’s lost the plot
author: Benjamin Riley
summary: Benjamin Riley explains why he is not listening to Emily Hanford's Sold a Story 2 podcast on direct instruction: after twenty years of visiting classrooms he thinks the proportion of direct instruction is a sideshow. He recalls once sharing the small-c conservative enthusiasm of the Science of Learning movement for teacher authority, but says regular classroom visits replaced ideology with complexity. To make the case he walks through three teaching videos. In a brisk chemistry lesson, observers praised the pedagogical moves while one asked whether students understood what bonding really means. A second, struggling lesson shows that delivery mode does not fix tasks that lack meaning. In the third, Dan Meyer's video of Ms. Bryant coaxing a disengaged student back into a math task, whether it is direct instruction hardly matters. Riley argues that what counts is whether students attend to meaning, that varying approaches probably helps attention, and that the real aim is humane, loving teaching. He ends by saying he would rather spend his energy defending public education than debating instructional mode.
points: Riley argues that the amount of direct instruction is a surface feature of teaching and matters far less than whether students pay attention to what is meaningful.
A polished, well-managed lesson can still leave open whether students understood the concept, so observers should ask about learning and not only about technique.
He suggests that interleaving lecture and inquiry is likely better for sustaining attention than devotion to a single approach.
The Ms. Bryant video is used to show that human relationship and steady, loving pressure are what bring a disengaged student back to thinking.
Riley frames the debate as shaped by ideology and by a chattering class with little classroom experience, and calls the podcast's focus a sideshow.
quotes: Very few of the edu-chatterers, myself included, have meaningful K-12 classroom teaching experience. As such, the chattering class tends to focus on systemic policy levers that can be pulled, or slightly more interestingly, debates about the ideology of education.
Ideological dispositions start to give way to complexities, ones that surface again and again and again. At least, this is what happened to me.
And the amount of direct instruction just isn’t that important, or even all that relevant, to meaningful student learning.
Are the students learning what bonding in compounds really means?
We interpret pedagogy through our existing values, and in a pluralistic country, our values are diverse.
The instructional mode of delivery is often just a surface feature of teaching. A compelling lecture might get students to pay attention to meaning, but a boring one will not.
it’s varying between the two, interleaving we might say, that will almost surely be better for maintaining attention versus slavish devotion to one approach or another.

Instead, we get sold a story that’s lost the plot. If we want more teachers to practice the radical empathy on display in Ms. Bryant’s interaction with Sam, and we should very much want that, direct instruction is not going to bring us one inch closer to that goal.
